```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Many interactions in education and work are carried out by actors of
different kinds: a learner and a tutor, a student and a generative AI
assistant, a programmer and a coding agent. A record of such an interaction
is a sequence of coded events in which the actors take turns, and the
questions it raises concern both what each actor does and how the actors
respond to each other. Transition network analysis (TNA) models a sequence of
events as a network whose nodes are the codes and whose weighted, directed
edges are the probabilities of moving from one code to the next. Applied to a
mixed sequence, ordinary TNA treats all codes alike and loses the
information that some codes belong to one actor and some to another.

Heterogeneous transition network analysis (HTNA) keeps that information. Each
code is assigned to one actor type, the network is estimated over the
interleaved sequence so that transitions within and between actors are
counted from the same events, and the actor partition is carried through
every subsequent step: the layout and colours of the plot, the summaries of
transitions within and between actors, and the patterns of turn-taking
(López-Pernas, Misiejuk, & Saqr, 2026). This vignette sets out the
formulation and follows one analysis from data to assessed conclusions.

```{r setup}
library(htna)
```

## The model

A session is a sequence of coded events $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_T$, and every
code $i$ belongs to exactly one actor type $a(i)$, for example Human or AI.
Counting, over all sessions, how often code $i$ is directly followed by code
$j$ gives the counts $n_{ij}$. The relative transition network has the
weights

$$w_{ij} = \frac{n_{ij}}{\sum_k n_{ik}},$$

the estimated probability that an event coded $i$ is followed by an event
coded $j$. The actor partition divides the weight matrix $W$ into blocks
$W_{AB}$, holding the transitions from codes of actor $A$ to codes of actor
$B$. The diagonal blocks ($A = B$) describe how an actor continues its own
turn, and the off-diagonal blocks describe the handovers between actors.
Because each row of $W$ sums to one, the row sum of code $i$ within block
$W_{AB}$, $\sum_{j:\,a(j) = B} w_{ij}$, is the probability that an event
coded $i$ is followed by an event of actor $B$. A meta-path is the sequence
of actor types that a path of codes passes through, such as
Human $\to$ AI $\to$ Human.

## Data

`human_ai` holds the coded turns of 429 sessions in which programmers worked
with an AI coding agent ("vibe coding"), from 34 projects. Each row is one
coded event; a message can carry several codes.

- **Session:** `session_id` identifies the sequence; transitions are counted
  within sessions.
- **Order:** `order_in_session` orders the events within a session.
- **Code:** `code` is the event code, six for the human (`Check`,
  `Frustrate`, `Inquire`, `Refine`, `Request`, `Specify`) and six for the AI
  (`Ask`, `Delegate`, `Execute`, `Plan`, `Repair`, `Report`).
- **Actor type:** `actor_type` (`"Human"` or `"AI"`) assigns each event to
  its actor.
- **Phase:** `phase` (`Early`, `Late`) splits the sessions chronologically
  in half; it is used in the grouped vignette.

```{r data}
with(human_ai, table(actor_type))
```

The 19,347 events consist of 10,796 human and 8,551 AI events.

## Building the network

The network is estimated with `build_htna()`, which takes the data and the
name of the column that assigns each event to its actor.

```{r build}
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
summary(net)
```

The network has 12 nodes, six per actor, and 135 of its 144 possible edges
are non-zero. Within the human codes 35 of the 36 possible transitions occur,
and in each between-actor block all 36. The AI block is the sparsest, with 28
non-zero edges: some AI codes rarely follow one another directly.

## How the actors hand over

The edge table lists every non-zero transition with the actor types of its
source and target, so that within-actor transitions and handovers can be read
side by side.

```{r edges}
head(as.data.frame(net))
```

Each row is one edge; for example, an AI `Ask` is followed by a human
`Frustrate` with probability 0.116 and by an AI `Plan` with probability
0.409. The counts per actor-pair block summarize the same table.

```{r actor-pairs}
as.data.frame(summary(net), what = "actor_pairs")
```

## The network plot

`plot_htna()` draws the network with the codes of each actor on their own
arc, in the actor's colour and shape; edges below 0.05 are not drawn.

```{r plot, fig.height = 6}
plot_htna(net)
```

Edge width is proportional to the weight, and only the 73 edges with a
weight of at least 0.05 are drawn (the same edges that the pruning step
below keeps), so the plot shows the transitions that carry the interaction.

## Which codes are central

Centralities rank the codes by their position in the network. In-strength is
the total transition weight flowing into a code, out-strength the weight
leaving it, and betweenness the number of shortest paths through it.

```{r centralities}
centralities_htna(net, measures = c("InStrength", "OutStrength",
                                    "Betweenness"))
```

`Execute` receives the most transition weight (in-strength 2.03) and lies on
the most shortest paths (betweenness 29), followed on in-strength by the
human `Request` (1.69). The out-strengths are all close to one because each
row of a relative network sums to one, less any self-transition. The
interaction is organized around the request-and-execute exchange.

```{r plot-centralities, fig.height = 5}
plot_centralities(net, measures = c("InStrength", "Betweenness"),
                  by = "group")
```

## Focusing on the strong transitions

Pruning sets weak edges aside so that the structure carried by the strong
transitions can be read.

```{r prune}
pruned <- prune_htna(net, threshold = 0.05)
as.data.frame(summary(pruned), what = "actor_pairs")
```

At a threshold of 0.05, 73 edges remain. The AI-to-human block keeps 27 of
its 36 edges, more than any other block, while the AI-to-AI block keeps 13:
after an AI action the next event is most often a human one.

## Turn-taking patterns

Meta-paths describe the order in which the actors take turns, regardless of
the specific codes.

```{r meta-paths}
extract_meta_paths(net, level = "type", length = 3)
```

The alternating meta-path Human $\to$ AI $\to$ Human is the most frequent
(3,593 occurrences in 402 sessions) and occurs 1.41 times as often as the
frequencies of the two actors would predict. Runs within one actor are rare
by the same standard: three consecutive human events have a lift of 0.46 and
three AI events of 0.25. The interaction is a dialogue of short turns.

A schema lists the concrete paths behind one meta-path.

```{r schema}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "Human->AI->Human"), n = 5)
```

The most frequent is a request, an AI execution and a further request (401
occurrences in 194 sessions, five times as often as expected), the iterative
loop of directing the agent.

## The sessions over time

The network pools the transitions of all sessions and positions. A sequence
plot shows the sessions themselves, one row per session and actor, with each
cell coloured by its code.

```{r sequences, fig.height = 5.5}
sequence_plot_htna(net, type = "heatmap")
```

## How certain are the edges

The bootstrap resamples the sessions and re-estimates the network to show
which edge weights the data determine precisely.

```{r bootstrap}
boot <- bootstrap_htna(net, iter = 100, seed = 1)
boot
```

With 100 resamples, 60 of the 135 edges are reproduced within the
consistency range and marked significant; the strongest, `Delegate` to
`Plan`, has a mean weight of 0.609 with a 95% interval from 0.541 to 0.670.
A real analysis would use the default 1,000 resamples. The plot draws the
non-significant edges dashed.

```{r bootstrap-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot_htna_bootstrap(boot)
```

## Are the conclusions stable

Two checks ask whether the conclusions depend on the particular sessions
observed. Centrality stability drops increasing shares of the sessions and
correlates the centralities with those of the full network (Epskamp,
Borsboom, & Fried, 2018).

```{r stability}
cs <- centrality_stability_htna(net, iter = 100, seed = 1)
as.data.frame(cs)
```

All three measures keep a correlation above 0.7 until 90% of the sessions
are dropped (CS coefficient 0.90), well above the recommended 0.5, so the
centrality ranking can be reported. Split-half reliability estimates the
network from two random halves of the sessions and compares them.

```{r reliability}
rel <- reliability_htna(net, iter = 100, seed = 1)
summary(rel)
```

The edge weights of the two halves correlate at 0.982 on average and differ
by 0.0125 on average, so the estimated structure does not depend on which
sessions happened to be observed.

- [Input formats](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/input-formats.html),
  [Comparing networks](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/comparing-networks.html),
  [Model assessment](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/model-assessment.html),
  [Markov-order adequacy](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/markov-order.html),
  [Sequences and patterns](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/sequences-and-patterns.html),
  [Frequencies and mosaic plots](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/frequencies-and-mosaic.html),

- Case studies: [early and late sessions of vibe coding](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/case-early-late.html)
  and [help-seeking in vibe coding](https://sonsoles.me/htna/articles/case-vibe-coding.html).
